claims.text: The equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy and the relevant quaternary and ternary subsets are single-phase FCC after similar thermomechanical processing.
Constituent count alone is inadequate to explain the alloys' mechanical-property differences.
Differences in local short-range order and magnetic interactions are the primary cause of the mechanical-property differences because they modify effective stacking-fault energy.
Adding Mn to form equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni produces magnetic frustration.
Mn encourages local chemical clustering in the quinary alloy.
Magnetic frustration and local chemical clustering lower the effective stacking-fault energy of the quinary alloy.
The reduced stacking-fault energy of the quinary alloy promotes early deformation twinning and possibly an FCC-to-HCP transformation.
Removing Mn in the quaternary and ternary subsets raises their effective stacking-fault energy.
Mn-free lower-element subsets have reduced magnetic frustration relative to the quinary alloy.
The lower-element subsets have less pronounced local chemical ordering than the quinary alloy.
Higher stacking-fault energy in the lower-element subsets suppresses twinning and favors dislocation slip.
The combination of twinning, slip, and possible phase transformation in the quinary alloy increases its work hardening and ductility.
Relative to the quinary baseline, the quaternary and ternary subsets will show delayed twin initiation or a lower twin density.
Relative to the quinary baseline, the quaternary and ternary subsets will have lower strain-hardening rates and earlier necking or failure.
The predicted compositional differences will be more pronounced at 77 K if magnetic interactions are significant.
The proposed mechanism applies only while the alloys remain single-phase FCC and stacking-fault energy dominates defect activity rather than secondary phases or other microstructural features.

contradictions.description: The material scope includes the quinary alloy's quaternary and ternary subsets generically, some of which retain Mn, but the causal comparison treats the lower-element subsets collectively as products of Mn removal. The stated mechanism therefore does not consistently cover the full declared subset population.
